sections.section_name: Section B - Very Short Analytical Concepts

questions.question_text: Define Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions for evaluating limiting molar conductivities. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Kohlrausch's law states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual ionic contributions of its constituent cations and anions at infinite dilution.

questions.question_text: Provide the fundamental structural reason for the phenomenon of lanthanide contraction across the f-block elements. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: Lanthanide contraction occurs due to the highly imperfect and poor shielding effect of inner 4f electrons, allowing the increasing effective nuclear charge to pull valence electrons closer, reducing atomic radii.

questions.question_text: State Raoult's law specifically for a binary solution containing a volatile solvent and a non-volatile solute. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: For a solution containing a non-volatile solute, Raoult's law states that the relative lowering of the solvent's vapor pressure directly equals the mole fraction of the dissolved non-volatile solute.

questions.question_text: Calculate the half-life ($t_{1/2}$) of a first-order chemical reaction if its specific rate constant is evaluated at $2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: For a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k}$. Substituting the rate constant yields $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}} = 346.5 \text{ s}$.

questions.question_text: Differentiate structurally between an ambidentate ligand and a standard monodentate ligand in coordination chemistry, providing one example. [20-30 words]
questions.answer: An ambidentate ligand is a monodentate ligand possessing two different donor atoms but binding through only one at a time. A classic example is the thiocyanate ion, $\text{SCN}^-$, binding via S or N.

questions.question_text: Derive the integrated rate equation for a zero-order chemical reaction taking the form $R \rightarrow P$. State the structural formula for its half-life. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: For a zero-order reaction, $\text{Rate} = -\frac{d[R]}{dt} = k[R]^0 = k$. Integrating $-d[R] = k \cdot dt$ gives $[R] = -kt + [R]_0$, where $[R]_0$ is initial concentration. The half-life is structurally derived as $t_{1/2} = \frac{[R]_0}{2k}$.

questions.question_text: Write the official IUPAC naming nomenclature for the coordination complex $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ and identify its exact primary and secondary valencies. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: The IUPAC name is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride. According to Werner's theory, the primary valency corresponds to the oxidation state, which is +3, and the secondary valency corresponds to the coordination number, which strictly equals 6.

questions.question_text: A current of $1.5\text{ A}$ is passed through an aqueous solution of $\text{CuSO}_4$ for exactly $10$ minutes using inert electrodes. Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. (Molar mass of Cu = $63.5\text{ g/mol}$, 1F = $96487\text{ C}$). [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Total charge $Q = I \times t = 1.5 \times 600 = 900\text{ C}$. The reduction is $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$. Thus, $2 \times 96487\text{ C}$ deposits $63.5\text{ g}$. Mass deposited $= \frac{63.5 \times 900}{2 \times 96487} = 0.296\text{ g}$.

questions.question_text: Construct the d-orbital crystal field splitting profile for an octahedral complex. Mathematically distinguish between high-spin and low-spin configurations using pairing energy ($P$) and crystal field splitting energy ($\Delta_o$). [30-40 words]
questions.answer: In an octahedral field, d-orbitals split into lower $t_{2g}$ and higher $e_g$ sets separated by $\Delta_o$. If $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field), electrons singly occupy $e_g$ before pairing, creating high-spin complexes. If $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field), electrons pair in $t_{2g}$, forming low-spin complexes.

questions.question_text: Determine the osmotic pressure in atmospheres of a solution prepared by dissolving $2.5\text{ g}$ of a polymer (Molar mass = $50,000\text{ g/mol}$) in $500\text{ mL}$ of water at $300\text{ K}$. ($R = 0.0821\text{ L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$). [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Calculate concentration $C = \frac{n}{V} = \frac{2.5 / 50000}{0.500} = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$. Applying the osmotic pressure formula $\pi = CRT$, we get $\pi = 10^{-4} \times 0.0821 \times 300 = 0.00246\text{ atm}$.

questions.question_text: Explain strictly why transition metals and their compounds predominantly act as excellent heterogeneous catalysts in industrial chemical kinetics. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Transition metals exhibit variable oxidation states and possess vacant d-orbitals. This allows them to easily form intermediate complexes with reactants, lowering the activation energy barrier, and provides a large active surface area for adsorption in heterogeneous catalysis.

questions.question_text: Calculate the boiling point elevation when $10\text{ g}$ of a non-volatile solute (Molar mass = $100\text{ g/mol}$) is completely dissolved in $200\text{ g}$ of benzene. Given $K_b$ for benzene is $2.53\text{ K kg mol}^{-1}$. [30-40 words]
questions.answer: Solute moles $n = \frac{10}{100} = 0.1\text{ mol}$. Solvent mass $= 0.200\text{ kg}$. Molality $m = \frac{0.1}{0.200} = 0.5\text{ mol/kg}$. The boiling point elevation is $\Delta T_b = K_b \cdot m = 2.53 \times 0.5 = 1.265\text{ K}$.

questions.question_text: Read the following kinetics case study: A nuclear chemistry laboratory tracks the radioactive decay of a Carbon-14 isotope sample, which rigidly follows first-order chemical kinetics. The initial activity of the sample is noted at 800 disintegrations per minute (dpm). After exactly 11,460 years, the activity drops to 200 dpm. Evaluate the decay constant ($\lambda$) and calculate the precise half-life ($t_{1/2}$) of the Carbon-14 isotope using integrated rate equations. [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Using the first-order rate equation $\lambda = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\left(\frac{A_0}{A_t}\right)$, we insert values: $\lambda = \frac{2.303}{11460}\log\left(\frac{800}{200}\right) = \frac{2.303}{11460}\log(4) = \frac{2.303 \times 0.602}{11460} = 1.209 \times 10^{-4}\text{ year}^{-1}$. The half-life is computed as $t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda} = \frac{0.693}{1.209 \times 10^{-4}} = 5730\text{ years}$.

questions.question_text: Read the following electrochemical scenario: An Apollo spacecraft utilizes a Hydrogen-Oxygen fuel cell to provide continuous electrical power while outputting pure water as a byproduct. The standard cell potential ($E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) for this galvanic operation is measured at $+1.23\text{ V}$ at standard state conditions. State the anodic and cathodic half-cell reactions in an alkaline medium, and calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$) for the overall reaction. (1F = $96487\text{ C}$). [40-50 words]
questions.answer: Anode reaction: $2\text{H}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + 4e^-$. Cathode reaction: $\text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + 4e^- \rightarrow 4\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$. Total electron transfer $n = 4$. Using $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}$, we get $\Delta G^\circ = -4 \times 96487 \times 1.23 = -474,716\text{ J/mol}$ or $-474.7\text{ kJ/mol}$.

sections.section_name: Section E - Long-Form Structural & Organic Synthesis

questions.question_text: A standard Daniel cell operates based on the redox reaction $\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}$. Standard potentials are $E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}$. Derive the overall standard cell potential. Then, using the Nernst Equation, calculate the specific non-standard electromotive force (EMF) of the cell at $298\text{ K}$ if the concentration of $[\text{Zn}^{2+}]$ is $0.1\text{ M}$ and $[\text{Cu}^{2+}]$ is $0.01\text{ M}$. Determine if the reaction remains spontaneous. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Standard cell potential $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\text{ V}$. The Nernst equation at $298\text{ K}$ with $n=2$ is $E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.0591}{2} \log\left(\frac{[Zn^{2+}]}{[Cu^{2+}]}\right)$. Substituting parameters: $E_{\text{cell}} = 1.10 - 0.02955 \log\left(\frac{0.1}{0.01}\right) = 1.10 - 0.02955 \log(10) = 1.10 - 0.02955 = 1.0704\text{ V}$. Since $E_{\text{cell}} > 0$, the reaction strongly remains spontaneous.

questions.question_text: Utilizing the framework of Valence Bond Theory (VBT), deconstruct the hybridization, structural geometry, and exact magnetic behavior of the hexafluoridocobaltate(III) ion, $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, and the hexaamminecobalt(III) ion, $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$. Contrast the roles of the fluoride and ammonia ligands in influencing inner versus outer orbital orbital utilization. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: In $[\text{CoF}_6]^{3-}$, Cobalt is $+3$ ($3d^6$). Fluoride is a weak field ligand, preventing electron pairing. It uses outer $4d$ orbitals, yielding $sp^3d^2$ hybridization, an octahedral geometry, and is highly paramagnetic (4 unpaired electrons). Conversely, in $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, ammonia is a strong field ligand, forcing inner $3d$ electron pairing. This yields $d^2sp^3$ hybridization, an octahedral geometry, and it is completely diamagnetic (zero unpaired electrons).

questions.question_text: Analyze the formation of non-ideal binary liquid solutions that exhibit strong positive and negative deviations from Raoult's Law. Detail the thermodynamic conditions pertaining to enthalpy ($\Delta H_{\text{mix}}$) and volume ($\Delta V_{\text{mix}}$) changes for each deviation type. Construct one molecular interaction example for both the positive and negative deviation frameworks. [50-60 words]
questions.answer: Positive deviation occurs when solute-solvent interactions (A-B) are weaker than pure component interactions (A-A, B-B). Here, vapor pressure increases, $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$ (endothermic), and $\Delta V_{\text{mix}} > 0$. Example: Ethanol + Acetone. Negative deviation occurs when A-B interactions are exceptionally stronger than A-A/B-B forces via bonding. Vapor pressure drops, $\Delta H_{\text{mix}} < 0$ (exothermic), and $\Delta V_{\text{mix}} < 0$. Example: Chloroform + Acetone (due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding).
